name: Chewing for jaw

lead: Chewing for jaw, often called jawmaxxing, means chewing hard gum such as mastic or tough foods to build the masseters, the muscles at the angle of the jaw. The payoff people want is a wider, squarer, more defined lower face.

The masseter is a skeletal muscle and enlarges with sustained use; medical literature describes enlarged masseters in people who chew gum constantly, clench or grind their teeth. Whether chewing also changes the underlying jaw bone or profile has not been tested in published trials.

paras: Users chew mastic gum or firm foods in regular sessions, usually combined with mewing, chin tucks and neck exercises, and often with fat loss so the jaw shows. Visible muscle change is reported over weeks to months.

Medical sources link constant chewing and clenching to jaw muscle fatigue and temporomandibular symptoms, and a study of 323 adolescent girls examined gum chewing and jaw symptoms. Enlarged masseters can make the face look wider or uneven. One forum user reports worn molars and a bloated-looking face after years of chewing.

angle.text: Chewing tough gum or food builds the masseters, which can widen and define the lower face. Masseter enlargement from heavy chewing is documented in muscle research; effects on jaw bone have not been studied.

lead: Chewing for jaw, also called jawmaxxing, is a practice in looksmaxxing communities in which people chew very hard gum, most often mastic-based gum, or tough foods to develop the jaw muscles and, according to proponents, the look of the lower face and jawline.[1][2][3] The idea is a direct chain: more chewing work, a larger and stronger masseter, a fuller, more defined angle of the jaw. It is usually combined with other routines such as mewing, chin tucks and neck training.[2][4]

The muscle part of the chain is recognised in medical references: the masseter, one of the strongest muscles of mastication, can enlarge in people who clench or grind their teeth or who chew gum constantly, and the enlargement is usually bilateral and painless.[5] Animal research has also found that harder diets are associated with a wider masseter and with changes in jaw bone structure in mice.[6] Whether chewing regimens change the jawline in people, or alter bone, has not been tested in published human trials.

From about 2023 the practice moved from forums onto TikTok and Instagram, where several companies sell mastic-based "facial fitness" gum and describe it as a way to build the jaw muscles.[3][7] Dentists and other clinicians quoted in news coverage say that heavy use can strain the jaw joint, and that the claims lack supporting research.[3][7]

paras: Practitioners chew tough gum or food for extended periods, often alongside other regimens. One looksmax.org routine lists daily mastic gum chewing in a chin-tucked position for about 30 minutes, mouth taping at night, hard mewing, neck stretching and training, and nose breathing.[2] Another thread presents a guide to jawmaxxing built around tongue posture and the idea that facial structure is moulded by forces applied over time.[1]

Companies selling facial gum say a session can last from 30 minutes to two hours, according to CBS News, which reported brands including Stronger Gum, Jawz and Rockjaw, with prices from about $2 for a 10-piece pack to $90 for a six-pack set.[3] The National's coverage added JawLiner, whose TikTok advertising uses before-and-after images.[7]

Hard gum is not the only form. Forum users also describe chewing tough foods, and some compare chewing with other jaw exercises. The practice sits within the broader vocabulary of looksmaxxing, in which a defined jawline is one of the features commonly discussed, and in which mewing and jaw surgery are other routes to the same goal.[8][4]

Mastic is a resin from the mastic tree (Pistacia lentiscus), traditionally produced on the Greek island of Chios, where it is called the tears of Chios. Wikipedia describes use of mastic in traditional medicine for about 2,500 years and notes that chewing it as gum is one of its earliest uses; the resin softens and turns white as it is chewed.[9]

In 2016 the European Medicines Agency judged that the clinical studies on mastic were too small and methodologically limited to support well-established use, while finding no significant safety concerns, and approved powdered mastic as a traditional herbal medicine for mild dyspepsia and minor skin inflammations and wounds.[9] Those uses are unrelated to jaw training; the EU protects the name Masticha Chiou with a protected designation of origin.[9]

Within looksmaxxing, mastic gum is often named together with Falim, a flavourless Turkish gum. A Substack writer who chewed Falim and Chios mastic for about seven weeks described the gum as rock hard at first, started with no more than ten minutes a day, later chewed about ten to fifteen minutes before bed, and reported that his jaw felt tired in the first nights and that he noticed a difference at the jaw corner. He offered no measurements and said the post was not sponsored.[10]

The masseter is a thick, roughly quadrilateral muscle with superficial, deep and coronoid parts, supplied by the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve. It raises the mandible to close the jaw and is one of the strongest chewing muscles.[5] Wikipedia notes that people who clench or grind their teeth, or who chew gum constantly, can develop an enlarged masseter, that the enlargement is usually bilateral and soft, and that it can make the face look wider or asymmetrical. Patients sometimes seek care because of how their face looks, and the condition can coincide with temporomandibular joint problems.[5]

A review of mastication assessment notes that the number of teeth, bite force and salivary flow influence how a person chews.[11] A study comparing electromyographic activity in jaw muscles during clenching, swallowing and chewing examined how muscle activation differs between these tasks under varying occlusal conditions.[12]

Some clinicians quoted in the press distinguish between the muscle and the jawline. One expert told The National that overusing the masseter can make it bulky, especially in slimmer people, which can widen the lower face rather than sharpen it.[7] Proponents, by contrast, treat a larger masseter as the goal, and a number of forum users post images of masseter hypertrophy as evidence the method works.[13]

Chewing as a jaw exercise has long been discussed in orthodontics and dentistry in the context of muscle function and growth, mostly in children and in animal experiments. In looksmaxxing forums it appears as one of the "bonehack" or jawmaxxing methods, alongside tongue posture practices descended from mewing, the orthotropics idea named after British orthodontist John Mew.[4]

Wikipedia reports that interest in mewing began rising on Google Trends in January 2019 and that it became widely covered through social media, especially in looksmaxxing circles.[4] Hard facial gum followed on the same platforms. By June 2024 CBS News was describing mastic-based facial gum as a TikTok trend tied to mewing and looksmaxxing, and The National covered it that August.[3][7] Companies cite research in their marketing: CBS reported that the founder of Rockjaw and the owner of Stronger Gum both pointed to a 2019 Tokyo Medical and Dental University study, with the Stronger Gum owner also describing his own jaw muscle growth after chewing the gum for less than a year.[3]
No studies found. No published human trial has tested chewing regimens, including facial fitness gum, for jaw or facial appearance.

Related research addresses other questions. A 2019 Tokyo Medical and Dental University study in Scientific Reports fed mice a harder diet and reported wider masseter muscles, more activity in the motor cortex region that controls chewing, and jawbone reshaping that the researchers linked to greater IGF-1 production by bone cells; it combined micro-CT imaging with a computer simulation of bone stress.[6] The study was in mice, not people.

A 2020 Frontiers in Physiology study from the same university compared 64 rats raised on normal chow with rats raised on a soft powdered diet after weaning. The soft-diet animals had smaller jaw opening and lower jaw-opening muscle activity at several ages, and the authors cautioned that the results may not transfer directly to humans.[14]

Human studies concern habits and symptoms. A questionnaire study of 323 girls aged 15 to 16 found gum chewing was very common (62.4%), with a mean of 3.95 hours per day among those who chewed, and examined its association with temporomandibular disorder symptoms.[15] A 1996 report examined gum chewing and jaw muscle fatigue and pain.[16] A systematic review studied the effect of malocclusion on jaw motor function and chewing in children.[17]

In the CBS News report, Edmond Hewlett, a UCLA dentistry professor and American Dental Association spokesperson, said most viral trends are rarely backed by scientific evidence. He said chewing dense gum for long periods could cause jaw pain and headaches and might raise the risk of temporomandibular disorders. The ADA was described as hesitant to say the products work, saying more research is needed.[3]

The National quoted dentist Abhijesh Chandran, who said the idea lacks authentic research and warned that sweetened gum can erode enamel and that regular chewing of hard gum can cause bite changes and temporomandibular joint disorders. Oral and maxillofacial surgeon Anurag Singh described a risk of TMJ overload and a bulkier masseter. Plastic surgeon Suhas S said he expected no effect and named surgery, threads, fillers and botulinum toxin as the options he considered effective.[7]

A looksmax.org user who said he had mewed and chewed mastic gum for years reported that his dentist described his molars as worn like those of an elderly person, and that his masseter hypertrophy made his face look bloated because of limited cheekbone width.[13] Medical sources link enlargement of the masseter to constant gum chewing and possible temporomandibular joint problems.[5]
The American Association of Orthodontists has said there is no current research showing that mewing benefits the jawline or oral health.[3][4]

Chewing is commonly combined with mewing and tongue posture, chin tucks, neck training and mouth taping in forum routines.[2][1] Other jawline approaches discussed in the same communities include masseter botulinum toxin, fillers, chin and jaw implants, and orthognathic surgery, which the press coverage and Wikipedia place under the "hardmaxxing" side of the culture.[7][8]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, chewing is discussed as one of the jawmaxxing methods with a plausible muscular effect, with members debating whether the result is desirable.[1][13]

timeline.event: Mastic resin from Chios is used in traditional medicine and as a chewing gum, for about 2,500 years according to Wikipedia.[9]
A report on gum chewing, jaw muscle fatigue and pain is published in the Journal of Oral Rehabilitation.[16]
A questionnaire study of 323 adolescent girls links oral habits including gum chewing with temporomandibular symptoms.[15]
The European Medicines Agency approves powdered mastic as a traditional herbal medicine for mild dyspepsia and minor skin conditions.[9]
Interest in mewing begins to rise on Google Trends in January; a Tokyo Medical and Dental University mouse study of forceful mastication is published in Scientific Reports.[4][6]
A Frontiers in Physiology rat study reports effects of a soft diet on jaw movement and jaw muscle activity.[14]
CBS News (June) and The National (August) report on mastic-based facial fitness gum spreading on TikTok and Instagram.[3][7]
